body.text: Despite a solid start, the Australian share market is struggling for direction and even slipped into negative territory in the first hour of trading.
Euphoria over AI profits boost Wall Street's tech stocks, driving the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to new record highs.

ASIC sues former financial adviser linked to First Guardian collapse
ASIC says it has commenced civil penalty proceedings against former financial adviser Osama Saad.

It alleges he carried out schemes to avoid conflicted remuneration laws and contravened his best interest obligations when providing financial advice to hundreds of clients to invest their superannuation into the First Guardian Master Fund (First Guardian), which later collapsed.
The corporate regulator alleges Mr Saad's entities, Atlas Marketing and United Capital, were paid about $34 million by entities connected to the Shield Master Fund (Shield) and First Guardian.
It alleges some of the money was used for Mr Saad's personal benefit and for the benefit of individuals and entities associated with him.

It also alleges some of the monies funded marketing and lead generation entities that referred thousands of clients to Venture Egg and Financial Services Group Australia. Those firms recommended clients invest their superannuation into Shield, First Guardian, or both.
You can read ASIC's press release here, which contains much more detail.
High Court rules in favour of climate group in Hunter Valley coal mine case
This will be worth following today as the story unfolds, given the implications it will have for Australia's mining and energy sectors.
The ABC's climate reporter Charlotte King writes:
"A landmark ruling in the High Court has found planning authorities are required to consider local climate change effects when approving fossil fuel projects.
"Three of the five judges found in favour of a Hunter Valley residents' group, which halted the Mount Pleasant mine expansion last year in the New South Wales Court of Appeal.
"The High Court has agreed with that judgement and found the project's planning approval needed to take into account local effects from climate change caused by emissions from its coal exports.
"The case is expected to have national implications for the way fossil fuel project approvals take global emissions and local climate change impacts into account."

Most sectors higher, but financials weigh on Australian share market
Now here's how all the ASX sectors are performing after the first hour.
Energy (+0.7%) and consumer discretionary (+0.5%) are making the biggest gains so far.
Though most sectors are relatively flat, including materials, tech, industrials and real estate.
Financials (-0.4%), in particular, the banks are lagging well behind.

ASX turns negative as Commonwealth Bank and Fortescue weigh on the market
After a mildly positive start, the share market has now fallen into the red.
The ASX 200 was down 0.06% to 8,899 points by around 10:55am AEDT, so it's practically flat.

Some of today's worst performers include drone company Elsight, family tracking app provider Life360, laser weapons business Electro Optic Systems and resource stocks like IperionX, Elvira Lithium, Champion Iron and Regis Resources.
Big names in the financial and materials sector are also down, including Fortescue (-1.6%), Bluescope Steel (-1.6%), Commonwealth Bank (-1.3%), Westpac (-1.1%) and AMP (-1%).

Just over half the stocks on the ASX 200 are trading higher today.
Companies that are linked with uranium mining or enrichment are seeing big increases in their share prices, including Deep Yellow, Silex Systems, Paladin Energy and NexGen Energy.

ASX up 0.2pc in early trade, most sectors trading higher
The Australian share market has started its day marginally higher.
The ASX 200 was up nearly 0.2% by 8,749 points by around 10:25am AEDT.
So far, the best-performing sectors are consumer discretionary (+0.7%), energy (+0.5%) and healthcare (+0.4%).
On the flip side, financials (-0.2%) and real estate (-0.1%) are weighing on the market.
Key Event
Coffee prices rise after card surcharge ban, RBA accused of kicking 'own goal'
The Reserve Bank has "kicked an own goal" by introducing the surcharge ban during a cost-of-living crisis.
That's according to Wes Lambert, CEO of the Australian Restaurant & Cafe Association, who my colleague Lin Lin interviewed for her latest story about Australia's card surcharge ban.
Meanwhile, former RBA assistant governor and Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis says any inflationary impact of the reforms will be temporary and unlikely to affect interest rates.
And there was some interesting data in the "Flat White Price Index", which tracks coffee prices at 1,500 cafes across Australia.
It found 17% of those cafes raised the price of a flat white since the surcharge ban was implemented on October 1.
The typical increase was 50 cents, or almost 10%.

Australian regulator launches probe into Chinese smart glasses company amid privacy fears
The Australian privacy commissioner has launched a formal investigation into the Chinese software company behind an influx of cheap smart glasses to Australia.

A recent ABC investigation found more than a dozen serious security flaws in the HeyCyan phone app used in smart glasses sold by Kmart, as well as online platforms such as Big W Marketplace and Amazon, among others.
Independent testing of the low-cost glasses found Australians' sensitive data, including email addresses, dates of birth, images and videos, were left exposed to hackers.
It also found the devices could be hijacked by nearby attackers without a password using only a Bluetooth connection, and that data was in some cases being sent to Chinese servers.
"The ABC's reporting … raised the prospect that there haven't been reasonable steps taken to secure [user] information," Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind said.

She said her office had "a range of concerns" about the practices of the company, Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co (Shenzhen Qingcheng), including about the possible use of facial recognition technology.

Paramount completes Warner Bros takeover to form media giant Skydance

Paramount has completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, uniting two of Hollywood's most storied studios in a media empire spanning television, news and cinema under the control of David Ellison.
The combined company, renamed Skydance, brings together Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures, the CBS News and CNN networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands.
Mr Ellison plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services over time.
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

The RBA is engineering an economic slowdown, but at what cost?
Our chief business correspondent Ian Verrender says interest rates will not be coming down any time soon because the world is undergoing a "massive epochal change".
On last night's episode of The Business, Ian said:
"For the past 35 years, we've had China basically exporting deflation because it became the world's factory. So it was producing more and more goods at cheaper prices.
"We've got greater defence spending because the world is no longer being a massive trading bloc. It's dividing itself into warring quarters in many ways.
"And on top of that, we've got an artificial intelligence boom.
"So all of these things combined are forcing up the cost of money."

Imported pork 'hiding in plain sight' on fast food giant Guzman y Gomez menu
Mexican fast-food chain Guzman Y Gomez (GYG) is under fire for advertising the use of Australian produce while importing hundreds of tonnes of Danish pork each year.
The company has confirmed it sources pork from Australia and Denmark for its burritos, tacos and other products.
GYG has defended its decision to use imported pork, saying it depends on "seasonal quality, availability and pricing".

Meanwhile, Australian Pork Limited (APL) is pushing for labelling laws similar to those that now apply to Australian seafood, requiring food chains and restaurants to declare where their product is from.

European stocks rise, bond yields fall as oil-driven inflation fears ease
European markets also performed well overnight, with Britain's FTSE and Germany's DAX rising 0.4% and 0.8%, respectively.
On Wall Street, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite rose to new record highs after shares of AI-related companies jumped.
One reason why markets are feeling optimistic is because inflation fears have eased slightly as oil prices stabilised around the $US100 per barrel mark, which is much lower than it has been lately.
Though, given the volatility in geopolitics, that relief could easily turn to "doom and gloom" at any moment, judging from how the US-Israeli war against Iran has played out in the past few months.
For now, investors are feeling less worried about oil-driven inflation, which led to global bond yields (or government borrowing costs) falling slightly.
Government borrowing costs slip
Long-dated US Treasury yields eased after touching fresh 24-year highs earlier this week, amid a persistent sell-off since late August on inflation and unsustainable debt concerns.
The US 10-year yield fell by 0.04 percentage points to 5.26%, while the 30-year yield dropped 0.03 percentage points to 5.63%.
Bond markets also found some respite after France's unpopular budget triggered a French debt sell-off and fuelled fears of broader stress across the euro zone.
France's 10-year bond yield dipped to 4.7% after surging to its highest since the 2000s last week.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in next spring's presidential election, outlined her plans to slash spending if elected in 2027.
Since yesterday evening, the Australian 10-year yield fell 0.06 percentage points to 5.35%.
In currency markets, the euro rose 0.4% to US1.13, stabilising after hitting a 17-month low in the previous session due to concerns about the euro zone's fiscal outlook.
The Australian dollar also fell marginally to 62 euro cents, after hitting a 22-month high against the European currency yesterday.

The RBA and the inflation myth. What many people don't get about price hikes
The Reserve Bank does not want consumer prices to come down, but to rise more slowly.
It's a common misunderstanding that the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) is responsible for, due to the confusing way in which it presents the inflation data every month.
In recent days, a video has done the rounds on social media of someone asking for help to understand what the RBA is up to. They said:

"If inflation means that prices are higher, does the RBA expect businesses to start reducing prices to make inflation decrease?"Because I don't see businesses ever reducing prices. I've never seen a company say that they'll permanently reduce their prices."So how does inflation actually get fixed?"
"If inflation means that prices are higher, does the RBA expect businesses to start reducing prices to make inflation decrease?
"Because I don't see businesses ever reducing prices. I've never seen a company say that they'll permanently reduce their prices.
"So how does inflation actually get fixed?"
That's a great question. And a perfect example of how a lot of people don't understand that falling inflation means prices going up, but at a slower rate.

Wall Street hits new record highs, ASX likely to drift along ...
Despite new record highs on Wall Street overnight, driven by AI enthusiasm, the Australian share market is likely to have a quiet start to the day.
ASX futures are flat, which suggests there might not be much movement, up or down, when the local trading day begins.
The Australian dollar rose slightly to 69.8 US cents.
What happened overnight?
On oil markets, Brent crude futures rose 0.7% to $US101.06 per barrel, which is lower than it's been these past couple of weeks.
Supply worries eased after the Group of Seven (G7) countries reached an agreement to release emergency diesel and crude stockpiles.
The not-as-high-as-before oil price led to US government bond yields, or borrowing costs, falling slightly as concerns about high inflation eased.
And that relief pushed the benchmark S&P 500 to its highest level ever, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite hit a new record high for its third straight day.

When oil prices stabilise or move lower, "that causes yields to move down because there's less anxiety about energy-driven inflation, which in turn is helping lift stocks higher," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York.
At the closing bell, the S&P 500 gained 0.6% to 7,820 points, the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.5% to 27,605 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average went up 0.5% to 51,532 points.
One of the best performing stocks was Marvell Technology, which climbed 5.8% after the chip designer lifted its revenue forecast for 2028 due to strong demand for its data center chips.
Meanwhile, chipmaker AMD gained 2.8% after CEO Lisa Su said the company planned to substantially increase chip supply this financial year to meet booming AI demand.
Anyway, please grab a coffee, tea, or whatever you like to have in the morning, and I'll be back with more updates shortly!
